title: There are only two effective biological interventions for adolescence depression.
subtitle: Most drugs don't work, an exploration of what now
body_html:
Child psychiatry is a grim discipline these days. For years, we've been studying how to treat children with depression. Only one medicine has evidence for efficacy. It's Prozac. Everything else has failed when we look at enough data.

I'm gonna apologize at the beginning of this article for not your references—I am at a conference, but there is a well referenced article at the bottom of this with links and references to the evidence.

You've heard about the mental health crisis in youth? Perhaps? 13% of high school girls will attempt suicide. 7% of high school boys will attempt suicide. That's in 2023. I doubt it it's better this year. We're not gonna fix that with a chat bot. We're not gonna fix that with drugs, because, as you'll remember me telling you, the largest data sets tell us they don't work.

Every oral medicine for adolescent depression comes with the black box warning from the FDA for increasing suicidal thoughts.

One of the problems with studies on adolescent depression drugs is they almost always rule out anyone who is suicidal.

Psychotherapy works, but that requires humans, and training, and remember how I told you 13% of adolescent girls attempt suicide? That means there are many more who are thinking about it, and need therapy. And we don't have enough Therapists. We don't pay enough for those Therapist. There will never be enough of those Therapists. There will absolutely never be enough child Psychiatrists. But, if our interventions basically don't work, and that includes every other drug you've ever heard about for adolescent depression. Just for shits and giggles, here's a list…

Paxil, Zoloft, Pixodrine, Lexapro, Celexa, nortriptyline, amitriptyline, vilazodone, venlafaxine. I made up Pixodrine.

There are more, but it doesn't matter. None of them work. Made up Pixodrine is as effective as anything that has an actual pharmacology.

You know what might work? Accelerated transcranial magnetic stimulation. We have an FDA label on once a day transcranial magnetic stimulation, which probably works, and doesn't have a black box warning for increasing suicide suicidal ideation.

We (as a healthcare system) should pay for that, routinely, and first line.

We should run to the studies on accelerated transcranial magnetic stimulation, because it's easier to tell a difference between two groups if we do it really quickly.

That's my rant, I'm at a conference, so I'm just gonna leave you at the next episode of the Carlat Report, where I make the above argument to Chris Aiken.

Thank you for reading.
